title: Bears coach Ben Johnson has urge to 'push the limits,' even as Caleb Williams develops "We’re starting all over again," said Johnson, who pointed to Caleb Williams and staff continuity as reasons to be excited. Jon Greenberg
summary:
Coach Ben Johnson expects the Bears to add a "layer of sophistication" this season. Greg Fiume / Getty Images
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — Ben Johnson had a nearly perfect debut season.
The Chicago Bears won 11 games, the NFC North and a home playoff game against the Green Bay Packers. Caleb Williams went from a polarizing rookie to a playoff hero and a Madden cover star. Johnson turned a hokey saying into a mantra and ripped off his shirt to earn the city free hot dogs.
Now, as his second season begins
full_text:
Coach Ben Johnson expects the Bears to add a "layer of sophistication" this season. Greg Fiume / Getty Images
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — Ben Johnson had a nearly perfect debut season.
The Chicago Bears won 11 games, the NFC North and a home playoff game against the Green Bay Packers. Caleb Williams went from a polarizing rookie to a playoff hero and a Madden cover star. Johnson turned a hokey saying into a mantra and ripped off his shirt to earn the city free hot dogs.
Now, as his second season begins in earnest with the opening of training camp, he wants to put the past where it belongs.
“I don’t think there’s talk about sustaining,” Johnson said Tuesday. “Shoot, we’re starting all over again. That’s been the consistent message.”
Johnson has indeed been beating that particular drum all offseason. It’s time to write some new music as his second camp gets underway at Halas Hall, where sustained success has been as ephemeral as franchise quarterbacks and new stadiums.
Of the four Bears coaches who preceded Johnson, three won either three or four fewer games in his second season. (Matt Eberflus improved from 3-14 to 7-10, but in Year 3, he went 4-8 and got fired.)
Eight years ago, the Bears were the darlings of the city, going 12-4 in Matt Nagy’s first season, and he was named coach of the year. The next year, after a distracting kicking competition and a regression by Mitch Trubisky, Nagy was just another bum of the week.
There were similarities between Nagy and Johnson in their first seasons — particularly with the rah-rah postgame speeches — but the key difference is that Johnson seems smarter and more self-aware. The two traits, I’ve found, often go together in a coach.
Like Nagy, Johnson inherited a highly touted quarterback. But the difference between Trubisky and Williams is simple: Williams is much better. Nothing makes an offensive whiz look smarter and more self-assured than a talented quarterback.
Johnson’s healthy relationship with Williams is why you should feel confident the Bears won’t backslide this season. They might not win 11 games with a first-place schedule and some key roster questions, but I think that with good health we’re going to see an improved offense and an even better Caleb. As for the overall roster, Johnson pointed to the “continuity” of the staff as one of many reasons to be excited going into camp after a middling offseason in terms of player acquisitions.
“Fortunately here, we were able to have a lot of the same faces come back, and with that I really expect another layer of sophistication to occur within this building and with our players,” he said.
Though he lost offensive coordinator Declan Doyle to the Baltimore Ravens, Johnson promoted passing game coordinator Press Taylor to take his place. But these are just titles. Johnson is the brains behind the scheme, and that is why teams with young quarterbacks desire offensive-minded head coaches. Johnson said he thought team chemistry was the Bears’ “secret sauce” last season. Maybe coaching cohesion will be this year.
It’s clear Johnson has a healthy ego, but he also seems to have the capacity for self-scrutiny. And maybe that’s why he’ll succeed where other Bears coaches have failed.
For example, in discussing Williams’ development Tuesday, Johnson said something that struck me as profound.
“I have this urge as an offensive guy to want to continue to evolve, and you can say innovate and push the limits a little bit,” he said. “And yet at the same time, in the back of my mind, what’s best for him is to continue to bank some of these reps. He’s had two offseasons and one training camp so far, and a full season obviously, to where he’s had a lot of the similar concepts repeat for him. And now we’re at the point where he’s not thinking about the play call, he’s not thinking about cadence, the motion, and all of the rigamarole before the snap. Things are starting to slow down.”
And as it works in sports, once things slow down, they speed up. The same goes for the coach.
Johnson said he still feels “like I’m drinking out of a fire hose” in this role. Going from offensive coordinator in Detroit to head coach in Chicago is a daunting leap in responsibility and fame. And in one year, Johnson became a hero in a city that puts football above everything. I’m not sure anyone in this city is more popular right now, with the possible exception being his quarterback.
While I believe that Johnson believes this season isn’t a continuation of the last, it’s not the reality for the rest of us. There is a lot of pressure on both of them to improve and excel, and if not make the Super Bowl, then at least to make an honest run toward it.
The regular season kicks off in six weeks. The Bears will start anew this morning. Johnson talked about a “physical” and “demanding” training camp with a gleam in his eye.
“This,” he said, “is where it gets fun.”

full_text:
Bears coach Ben Johnson promises another ultraintense training camp. “Anything worth doing is going to be challenging,” Johnson says. Kamil Krzaczynski / Imagn Images
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — Ben Johnson was still a few hours from delivering his first full training camp address to Chicago Bears players Tuesday at Halas Hall. So a few minutes before 1 p.m., he wasn’t about to clumsily drop any spoilers about the edge he’d be urging his team to adopt.
“That,” Johnson said with a wide grin, “is for team meetings. We’ll keep that there.”
Still, from the look in his eye, it seemed obvious Johnson was eager to deliver that first blast of messaging to a Bears team positioned to pursue grand achievements this season. And three minutes into his first camp Q&A with the media, it was also clear Johnson was in his usual driven headspace, standing at a lectern inside the PNC Center with energy and passion as the curtain rose on what promises to be a fascinating few months.
Johnson is promising another ultraintense training camp, in his words Tuesday, “a demanding ordeal” that will frequently push players to their mental and physical limits.
“Anything worth doing is going to be challenging,” Johnson explained. “These guys all know that, and I think they embrace it as well.”
Johnson reiterated that last season is ancient history, with the coach emphasizing — as he first did in January — how little the feel-good accomplishments of 2025 mean in this next phase of the team’s journey.
“You talk about sustaining success? Well, shoot. We are starting all over again,” Johnson said. “That’s been the consistent message.”
And that message has been accompanied by familiar reminders for players to understand what the coaches are looking for as they push to mold a team in the head coach’s vision, a unit that is consistently physical, poised and sound.
A push to grow closer is also part of the Bears’ agenda for the next six weeks. To that end, a pair of three-night trips to Cincinnati and Nashville, Tenn., for joint practices and preseason game action will offer bonding opportunities.
“We are in a race right now,” Johnson said, “to develop the same chemistry we had a year ago. I think that was one of the things that was our secret sauce: guys playing for each other. We had a really close-knit group.”
Much of Johnson’s second season in Chicago, of course, will still revolve around how much he can squeeze out of quarterback Caleb Williams, whose developmental leap from the beginning of training camp in 2025 to the end of the team’s playoff run in January was impressive. Still, Williams has many more checkpoints to pass through on his way to becoming one of the league’s best quarterbacks. And Johnson’s goal is to guide him as far as possible this season.
On that front, the connection between the two can be characterized as strong and growing stronger, which wasn’t always the case last summer when Williams himself acknowledged that, on many days, he was worried about how Johnson felt about him while also acknowledging he felt like he was “drowning, trying to breathe, stay alive and wait for a boat to come around.”
Now Williams stands in a much more comfortable posture at the helm of the Bears’ offense with Johnson guiding him and pushing him to become a better decision-maker, a more precise passer and a more efficient quarterback overall.
Throughout the spring, Johnson watched Williams polish his footwork, working on alignment to the target to enhance his accuracy. Training camp will present new challenges — and growth opportunities — in a different forum.
“When you get into the bullets flying and to where we’ve got full-speed reps here with O versus D, I think that’s where the ability (for him) to see, ‘Where should I go with the football?’ the process (becomes) a little bit faster,” Johnson said. “I’m hopeful we see another step in terms of the processing speed because we do have these banked reps at this point.”
Since Johnson arrived, Williams has made it clear he wants to be consistently pushed by his head coach. And hard. That Johnson, with his rare blend of honesty and drive, so naturally found the right buttons to push with Williams has been encouraging.
When general manager Ryan Poles was asked Tuesday why he believes the Johnson-Williams relationship has clicked, he kept it as simple as he could. “They both want to be great and win Super Bowls,” Poles said. “And that’s all that matters.”
The goal now is to bring an entire organization along for the ride. Which is why Poles, like his head coach, pushed back on the assertion that the Bears might be adjusting this year from being the hunter to becoming the hunted.
“It’s important,” Poles said, “to have that mindset that you’re always hunting.”
That won’t be an issue for Johnson, who seemed genuinely enthused by the realization that 42 players on his current 90-man roster weren’t here last season.
“As a coaching staff, we will apply pressure and stress on these guys,” Johnson said. “I think that’s where the best version of yourself comes forward.”
The first camp practice begins early this morning. And with that, the race will be on. Johnson, though, seems confident his squad will be in the proper attacking mindset with a full understanding of what’s ahead.
“This is where it gets fun,” he said. “This is our chance to forge our identity.”

full_text:
Jalen Davis, right, will try to keep his starting nickel spot while DJ Turner II, left, has solidified his place as one of the Bengals' starting outside cornerbacks. Sam Greene / Imagn Images
CINCINNATI — The Cincinnati Bengals open training camp Wednesday with a fair amount of competition and opportunity across the roster.
For the Bengals, the difference between this year and the last two camps is that the competition largely comes behind established starters rather than in search of them.
Rookies and unproven incumbents were thrust into starting roles at offensive line, edge rusher and linebacker last year. The inexperience showed and, other than Joe Burrow’s toe injury, it was the leading cause of the 2025 campaign’s failure.
This year, the 25 starters across offense, defense and specialists are almost all established, with track records that offer a measure of predictability.
The 2026 camp battles will come at depth positions, some of which are more important than others.
Here’s a closer look at the positional battles that need answers over the next six weeks, and how the team is approaching the competitions.
Background: The top two are locked: DJ Turner II and Dax Hill will start on the outside. Both head coach Zac Taylor and defensive coordinator Al Golden emphasized Monday that Hill will stay outside. Jalen Davis took over as the starting nickel corner down the stretch last year, and he played well enough to be penciled in as the incumbent starter there this season. A collection of rookies, journeymen and unproven younger players are all in the mix to fill out the remaining roles.
The battle: Every corner position beyond the two starting outside spots is up for grabs. That includes Davis’ nickel spot and the two backup positions. The battle royale for them features DJ Ivey (2023 seventh-round pick, 195 career defensive snaps), Tacario Davis (2026 third-round pick), Ja’Sir Taylor (127 defensive snaps with the Los Angeles Chargers and New York Jets last year), Josh Newton (2024 fifth-round pick) and Brayln Lux (2025 undrafted free agent with 19 career defensive snaps). Also, throw in third safety Kyle Dugger as another potential option.
What’s at stake: A typical season projects anywhere from 1,000 to 1,500 defensive snaps manned by cornerbacks beyond the top two.
Team view: This is considered the most important and wide-open positional battle in training camp. The corners behind Hill and Turner will have a significant role, and the Bengals don’t know much about any of them.
“Well, we’ll see once camp gets going,” de facto general manager Duke Tobin said. “Who is up to it and who is in the playbook and who is providing consistency and who has developed from last year? We are not going to pigeonhole anybody. The group as a whole, I was really impressed as I watched them move around in practices this offseason. We got a lot of guys with versatility that can play inside, outside.”
One name that drew praise from Tobin, Taylor and Golden was Ivey, who thrived in 115 snaps last season, mostly covering tight ends on third downs.
“We talk with players all the time: ‘If you want more roles, master your current one,’ Golden said. “That’s what DJ Ivey did last year. He came through for us. Certainly he warrants a more extensive look.”
Outlook: Anybody’s guess. Truly, these spots are up for grabs. No combination of names behind Hill and Turner should surprise anybody on the final 53 in September. The history with Jalen Davis, praise given to Ivey and draft capital used on Tacario Davis might give them an early advantage=-0, but this will be a best-man-wins camp.
Background: Demetrius Knight Jr. and Barrett Carter are entrenched as the starters. That statement alone brings trepidation for anyone who watched the Bengals’ defense capsize at the midpoint of last season. Both improved down the stretch, and the additions in front and behind them should help, but that doesn’t lessen the importance of establishing during camp that both can handle the job despite rookie struggles.
Behind them are 31-year-old veteran Oren Burks, 29-year-old journeyman Joe Giles-Harris and 26-year-old Shaka Heyward, a former UDFA with 48 career snaps.
What’s at stake: The largest leap of faith in the defensive rebuild. Do Knight and Carter look less like the lost, rattled rookies they were last season, and can they hold down the center of the defense? The development the team expects from them needs to show itself quickly, or else the Bengals’ personnel department must get to work hunting deals for a veteran insurance policy.
Team view: The united front of support for Carter and Knight continued Monday at the Bengals’ media luncheon. Tobin reiterated the plan wasn’t to avoid adding to the group this offseason, but with the anticipated development of the 2025 draft picks, the team prioritized other positions.
“We believe in the group that we have,” Tobin said. “We added competition in other areas. It’s hard to say you have established vets at all 22 spots. You are not going to have that in this league. You have to have guys compete for those roles and grow into the roles. Now they are the established vet. You have to develop guys within. We have guys that can develop, and we have guys we believe in and guys that played a lot early in their career. Guys that are comfortable in the scheme, comfortable with their teammates and understand the NFL and how it goes. We feel good about that group right now.”
An interesting admission came Monday from special teams coordinator Darrin Simmons, who expressed his confidence in the trio of backup linebackers. Their jobs will mostly be solidified by special teams performance, and he says Burks, Heyward and Giles-Harris are essential to his operation.
“I feel really good about the backups we have there, and their ability to do exactly what we need to do,” Simmons said. “That is a position that has been a little bit in flux for us the last couple of years, but in terms of the backups, I feel that is the strong suit of our core special teams unit.”
Outlook: Unlike cornerback, the battle at this position doesn’t feel wide open. The roles feel entrenched. The real competition here is Carter and Knight against themselves. If they look hesitant and appear to be the same players from last season’s ugly moments, the Bengals could quickly find themselves navigating a defensive crisis with no easy answer. The team expressed confidence those two will be fine at every turn; we will quickly see if that assessment was correct.
Background: The starting five return for the first time since Burrow’s arrival in Cincinnati. The interior looks solid, with Jalen Rivers back after an encouraging rookie season and two draft picks used to establish interior depth .
The battle will be held behind starting tackles Amarius Mims and Orlando Brown Jr. Cody Ford stands as the leader in the clubhouse, but the third and fourth spots are still unclaimed. Practice squad players from last year, Javon Foster and Andrew Coker, will be in the mix, along with a pair of rookie undrafted free agents. Also, sixth-round pick Brian Parker played tackle at Duke, but projects inside as a pro.
What’s at stake: Not much, just protecting the franchise player. Sarcasm aside, being one injury away from playing tackle in the Bengals’ pass-heavy scheme might be as important as some starting spots on this roster. Mims and Brown played every game last year, but both have injury histories, and there are no guarantees even if they didn’t.
Team view: Tobin notably pushed back against the idea that offensive line depth is an issue. He expressed confidence in the state of the competition and the level of investment behind the starting group.
Offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher will be closely monitoring the most notable position battle on his unit.
“That’s a question that we will have a lot better answer to in a month’s time,” Pitcher said. “The good thing is we have a lot of opportunity for guys to go show…

full_text:
Browns quarterbacks Shedeur Sanders, left, and Deshaun Watson will compete for the starting job in training camp. Nick Cammett / Getty Images
There are decisions to make at quarterback for the Cleveland Browns, which isn’t much different than many of the previous seasons since the team returned to the NFL in 1999. This is a franchise perpetually searching for answers it can’t seem to find. It’s quite possible this season isn’t much different in that regard.
As the curtain goes up on training camps across the NFL this week, the Browns have a good, old-fashioned quarterback competition between Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders about to begin. May the best man win. Or maybe the one with the best camera crew, since both candidates — who each ranked among the worst in the league the last time they were on the field — released their own hype videos this week.
I don’t have much faith in Sanders evolving into a franchise quarterback, but if you’re forcing me to choose between him and Watson, there isn’t much of a choice at all.
Two things are true: I fully expect Watson to win the starting quarterback job coming out of camp, and I have no interest in watching him take another snap for this team.
Watson missed 700 days between the time he left the Houston Texans and his debut in a Browns uniform, which was delayed by his 11-game suspension in 2022 after accusations of sexual misconduct and assault. He ultimately settled more than 20 civil suits against him and paid a $5 million fine to the NFL. He was lousy when he returned following the extended absence.
Well, here we are again. Should Watson start the opener against the Jacksonville Jaguars, it will mark 693 days since he last played in the NFL. He has two Achilles tears to blame this time. In all, Watson has played in 19 games in the 1,417 days since the season opener in 2022. We have more than enough evidence to know we’ve seen enough.
The trade to acquire him and the contract he was handed have been disasters. Owner Jimmy Haslam acknowledged as much. The Browns are nothing if not stubborn, so here we go again pushing this $230 million boulder up the side of the mountain and expecting at some point to draw blood from it. It’s far more likely the stone just crushes everything in its path. Again.
The term sunk cost fallacy means nothing in Berea. I don’t pretend to understand this team’s fascination with trying to squeeze some return out of a bad investment. Even if Watson managed to stay healthy and play moderately decent football this season, is there any chance they give him another contract? The answer had better be absolutely not, which makes playing him feel like an enormous waste of time.
While the Browns play out the final months of Watson’s contract, it’s worth noting that the Tampa Bay Buccaneers appear to have reached the same conclusion the Browns once did regarding Baker Mayfield. Watson is here because the Browns did not trust Mayfield enough to invest in him like a franchise starter. It’s happening all over again in Tampa. Despite Mayfield’s productivity the last couple of years, the team failed to reach terms on an extension with him this week, meaning Mayfield will be a free agent after the season when the Browns could again be shopping for a quarterback. Time is a flat circle.
Sanders, meanwhile, remains a work in progress. We’ll soon discover how much improvement he actually made over the summer. He has to make better — and quicker — decisions with the football. He has to get the ball out faster. He held onto the ball an average of 3.19 seconds last year, according to TruMedia, longer than any starter in the league. It remains to be seen whether new coach Todd Monken can sculpt an offense that plays to either of these quarterbacks’ strengths, but in Sanders’ case, making quicker decisions with the ball is essential to any sustained success.
There is plenty to like about what the Browns have done the last two years in digging out of their past mistakes and reshaping this roster. The Myles Garrett trade, while painful, was the responsible thing to do. Last year’s draft was an excellent start at assembling a roster foundation, and this draft appears to be another step. Now they have to do it on the field.
But it’s hard to take the Browns seriously in the AFC until they get adequate quarterback play, and it’s difficult to envision anyone on this roster delivering that. More than likely, they’ll be back in the draft again next year searching for another answer.
For now, someone has to take the snaps. Sanders at least provides the opportunity of the unknown and perhaps a glimmer of hope. Watson is the stone blocking the path.

title: Could George Pickens 'be a Cowboy for the rest of his career'? Jones also likes the "perception" that the Cowboys have had a "quiet offseason" — especially compared with recent offseasons. Jon Machota
summary: Could George Pickens 'be a Cowboy for the rest of his career'? Jones also likes the "perception" that the Cowboys have had a "quiet offseason" — especially compared with recent offseasons. Jon Machota
full_text:
The way Jerry Jones talked Tuesday, George Pickens definitely is in the team's long-term plans. Grant Halverson / Getty Images
OXNARD, Calif. — Jerry Jones has the reputation of being the most media-friendly owner in professional sports. The Dallas Cowboys owner and general manager has been significantly criticized since purchasing the franchise in 1989 for how much he speaks with reporters.
But it’s been a while since Jones gathered with the team’s local reporters to have a group interview session. He did so Tuesday, alongside executive vice president Stephen Jones and head coach Brian Schottenheimer for the team’s annual news conference to mark the start of training camp.
Jones’ previous news conference was at the end of the team’s draft in late April. His public silence has been part of what has been an abnormally quiet Cowboys offseason.
“I like the idea that the word is that we have had a quiet offseason relative to, dare I say, off-the-field noise or chatter, whatever you want to call it,” Jones said during what ended up being a 41-minute news conference followed by an 8 1/2-minute walk-off interview session. “I like that. That hasn’t been the case. We’ve had a lot going on and we’ve had to really scramble a lot, the kind of stuff that you don’t see. But it should be that way. It’s supposed to be hard. But we’ve had a very active (offseason). We have made a lot of decisions. We have made a lot of difficult decisions in my mind.
“I do like the perception that we’ve had a quiet, uneventful offseason, and let’s see how we can work in that. Perception is big. But what I will tell you is I don’t plan on doing anything around here for the next few days to stir anything up.”
Last year at this time, Jones was often asked about Micah Parsons and his contract situation. The All-Pro pass rusher attended training camp but did not practice. Things got ugly in the weeks that followed, and Parsons was traded to the Green Bay Packers a week before the season opener. The year before, star wide receiver CeeDee Lamb did not attend the California portion of training camp as he was seeking a new contract. Heading into the 2023 season, All-Pro right guard Zack Martin had a similar contract holdout.
This year has been much different. Although there was the possibility of something similar with standout wide receiver George Pickens, he signed the franchise tag, attended minicamp and is in Oxnard for the start of training camp.
Jones didn’t field one Pickens question until the 25-minute mark of Tuesday’s news conference.
“He’s a valued part of our aspirations and our potential success,” Jones said. “The combination that he has with the other talent on the team, I think, will make you feel pretty positive about what we’ve got a chance to do. I hope that he comes out here and is the most prolific, successful receiver in the NFL this year. And how would you like to be a free agent and with his credentials and step out there and have a year like that? I wish all of that because if that happens, that (would be) good for us.
“This can be a very win-win thing that we’ve done here, us and George being on the team. Make no mistake about it, George could be a Cowboy for the rest of his career, and that’d be a long time. Make no mistake about it. This (franchise tag) just fit for us and thank goodness it fit for him and we got it done.”
Jones’ optimism for the season led to him talking about Super Bowl aspirations and potentially making a “substantive” move to upgrade the roster.
Stephen Jones also shared his thoughts on where the roster sits entering camp. Notably, Dallas isn’t expected to have a player on the physically unable to perform list or the non-football injury/illness list to start camp. Players held out of organized team activities and minicamp because of recent surgeries, such as edge rusher Donovan Ezeiruaku (hip) and cornerback DaRon Bland (foot), are expected to be full participants.
“I think there’s always moves that you can make to be better,” Stephen Jones said. “I mean, we’re entertaining thoughts on players as we speak right now. I mean, (vice president of player personnel Will McClay) does an amazing job of getting the players and putting them in front of Jerry, myself and Schottenheimer. So we’re always looking for ways to get better. I will say that I think we’ve done a good job of putting together a roster that’s going to take the field (this week).
“I do feel like we’ve done a really good job of doing the things that we need to do to improve not only coaching, but also players to give us that opportunity. But, no, we’re not finished. We’re going to look for opportunities every day to improve this roster.”
In regard to keeping players on the current roster well beyond this season, Stephen Jones said defensive tackle Quinnen Williams is a high priority.
Dallas traded first- and second-round picks to the New York Jets last November to acquire the four-time Pro Bowler, who has two years left on his contract.
“We’re very open to that,” Stephen Jones said of a contract extension for Williams. “We want Quinnen here for the long haul. Obviously we’ve got a lot of resources tied up in him, and he knows what we think about him. We’ve had some discussions with the agent about how to go about the process, but certainly he’s one of the best in the business and we know kind of what that market is. Obviously it evolves and changes with each new deal, which is the case at any position. But certainly he’s at the top of the list in terms of people that we want to keep around here long term.”
Dallas’ offensive line has questions that need to be answered. The Cowboys would love for 2024 first-round pick Tyler Guyton to have a strong camp and solidify his spot as their starting left tackle. But if that doesn’t happen, look for All-Pro left guard Tyler Smith to move out to left tackle. That would weaken their interior, but their hand could be forced.
Schottenheimer said Tuesday that Smith will start at left guard but get tackle reps. He added that right guard Tyler Booker will get work at center.
New defensive coordinator Christian Parker was also a topic as he enters his first training camp as an NFL D-coordinator. There’s been a lot of praise for how he has handled things behind the scenes. He now gets a chance to put it on display against an offense that should be one of the league’s best.
“The way you know he’s an elite coach is when you walk by his office, and players, I mean multiple players, are in there wanting to listen and talk to him about scheme and things like that,” Schottenheimer said. “But the organization, the way he’s organized this camp on the defensive side of the ball, from the individual section to the tackling circuit drills, to the ball-disruption drills, to the install packages from first- and second-down fronts, pressures, coverages, things like that. He is a first-time coordinator that doesn’t act like a first-time coordinator. … (He’s) maybe the hardest-working coach I’ve ever been around.”
The Cowboys will hold their first training camp practice today. The first practice in full pads is Monday.

full_text:
Quarterbacks J.J. McCarthy, left, and Kyler Murray are competing to be the Vikings' starter, and it remains unclear when a decision will be made. Abbie Parr / Associated Press
EAGAN, Minn. — They seem comfortable living in limbo.
For months, the Minnesota Vikings extolled the virtues of a quarterback competition. Fiery practices would maximize performance. The hoopla surrounding every throw and decision would demand a high degree of focus and consistency.
Coach Kevin O’Connell designed this quarterback duel between Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy to bring out the best in a position that influences all of the other elements of the team.
Given the lack of full-speed practices this spring, the QB development effort runs parallel to the broader preparation of the offense. That ends Wednesday when training camp officially begins. Rep counts shrink. Opportunities are fewer. The Vikings use a rhythm- and timing-based system that requires humid days like these for players to get the right feel.
This spotlights perhaps the most fascinating push-pull of training camp.
How will O’Connell, general manager Nolan Teasley and the rest of the Vikings staff make a comprehensive decision on whether Murray or McCarthy will be the starter? And how will they balance the time it takes to pick their man with the time it takes to ensure that player has an adequate grasp of the team’s offensive operation?
“Having gone through training camps at that position,” O’Connell told reporters Tuesday, “I’m well aware of the time it takes to go into Week 1 comfortable and ready to get off to a really good start.”
This mindfulness explains why the Vikings are entering Wednesday’s opening practice with a planned timeline, which is subject to change depending on what the coaches observe on and off the field.
When are they scheduled to pick a starter for Week 1?
“I can’t remember it right now,” O’Connell said, smiling.
O’Connell met with all of the team’s quarterbacks this week to discuss the plan. Some of the highlights: Murray and McCarthy will get snaps with the first- and second-team offenses. Early on, practices will feature a 50-50 rep split, but that will change as practices morph into more realistic simulations. Executing the offense with command and precision remains the No. 1 priority.
Joint practices with the Baltimore Ravens kick off Aug. 19. Considering how much O’Connell values those practices as benchmarks for the team, it is fair to view that period as a pivotal point in the calendar. The Vikings could name a starter beforehand to give that player the more important reps. Or, if the competition shows little separation, O’Connell and company could use those practices to finalize their evaluation.
Neither O’Connell nor Teasley offered any clues about a preferred favorite Tuesday.
Teasley, though, did say he was “excited” about seeing Murray in O’Connell’s well-choreographed offense.
“He was the No. 1 pick for a reason,” Teasley said of Murray. “It’s not just about what he can do with his arm, and we all know he can operate on schedule … rarely do things go as planned in the National Football League, so it’s the extension of the play, and what he can do in that arena. He can create as well.”
This is where the conversation typically flows to the melding of Murray’s stylistic preferences with O’Connell’s complex offense.
Murray entered the league in 2019. With Murray on the field, the Arizona Cardinals set up in the shotgun on 85.3 percent of their snaps. Contrast that number with O’Connell’s Vikings, who have used the shotgun on only 53.1 percent of snaps.
Minnesota’s pre-snap process stresses the quarterback in ways Arizona’s didn’t. O’Connell’s offense also deploys many deep-drop concepts.
Since 2022, when O’Connell arrived, Vikings quarterbacks have taken 516 hits — the most of any team in the league by a sizable margin. Not even McCarthy’s potential growth as a layered passer or continued jelling with the locker room would allow for a major leap if he continues to sustain that level of punishment. This emphasizes two less sexy subjects than quarterback: improved offensive-line play and a revamped run game.
O’Connell and Teasley singled out both areas Tuesday. O’Connell even suggested the Vikings would commit to a more physical training camp than in past years to create more of an edge among the offensive linemen.
All of these factors matter in what the 2026 team becomes. Left tackle Christian Darrisaw’s availability remains a question. Safety Harrison Smith’s undecided future will affect the defense’s ability to deceive. First-round pick Caleb Banks’ health will factor prominently in the defense’s ceiling.
But for better or worse, all of these layers will take a back seat until the quarterback situation is settled.
“Whenever that happens,” O’Connell said, “that’s not the end-all. We need to continuously chase improvement amongst our whole team.”
The Vikings are betting the improvement can happen in a short time. Given the way the 2025 season went, and given the hard truth the Vikings haven’t won a playoff game since 2019, that bet had better be right.

full_text:
The New York Giants are taking over West Virginia's The Greenbrier Resort for two weeks. Johnny Sweet / The Athletic
WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — Twenty-four hours before New York Giants players, coaches and much of their staff arrive, The Greenbrier Sports Performance Center bustles.
Forklifts buzz around the parking lot. Police, team security and staff complete a security walkthrough of the fan section. Other staff are arranging the final pieces of Giants-branded fencing. The fields are chalked, the goalposts set, but instead of a New York City skyline and MetLife Stadium lurking in the background, West Virginia’s picturesque Allegheny Mountains provide the backdrop.
Situated within the 11,000-acre Greenbrier Resort, the performance center is already set up to resemble the Giants’ practice facility, with locker nameplates mounted, T-shirts hanging and more gear being added to the personalized cubicles. In the equipment room, every bit and bob that goes into outfitting a football player is neatly organized as the advance crew works into the final 24 hours to prepare the facility for nearly two weeks of NFL training camp.
But in the late afternoon, there’s a brief pause to pass out team ball caps to the folks from Clancy Relocation and Logistics, who’ve helped move the Giants from their home base in East Rutherford, N.J. to the mountains of West Virginia for their 12-day stint.
“Welcome to the Giants,” says one team staffer to the moving crew, which draws a round of applause.
That squad might not be suiting up for the team’s first practice Wednesday, but they’ve played an instrumental role in helping to make coach John Harbaugh’s first Giants training camp a success.
“Our whole goal is when they show up, they can just focus on all the things that they’re great at and that they need to focus on,” Megan Rosburg, assistant to the head coach/defensive assistant and the team’s point person for the excursion to West Virginia, told The Athletic this week.
Contrary to some initial rumors, conducting camp away from East Rutherford, N.J., wasn’t Harbaugh’s idea. In fact, the team signed a contract with The Greenbrier last fall, as plans for the West Virginia excursion have been in motion for more than a year due to a major multiyear expansion of the team’s facilities that the Giants announced this week. The recently concluded FIFA World Cup added to the offseason action, with MetLife Stadium hosting a handful of games, including the World Cup final.
Announcing our Football Operations Facility & Headquarters Expansion!
Details: https://t.co/R54s5SJ2SS pic.twitter.com/zR2Z6QJ5fz
— New York Giants (@Giants) July 27, 2026
So, the Giants have known they’d be on the road for a while, and this trip marks their first training camp outside of East Rutherford since heading to Albany, N.Y., in 2012.
But why did they pick a resort nearly 500 miles away in West Virginia? Why The Greenbrier?
Largely, because The Greenbrier has proven up to the task many times before.
In 2014, then-New Orleans Saints coach Sean Payton worked with the resort to establish a facility equipped for an NFL training camp. In the years since, the Denver Broncos, Houston Texans, Cleveland Browns, San Francisco 49ers, New England Patriots and Arizona Cardinals have used the facility for training camp or other parts of the NFL season. This year, the venue even hosted Iraq’s national soccer team as part of the World Cup. Rosburg spoke with Abir Chaudhry, the Browns’ director of team logistics and operations, to learn how the team got the most out of its time at The Greenbrier, from small details like outfitting player lounges and commute patterns to the big-picture planning of making the excursion as easy as possible.
“Everyone I’ve talked to is just super enthusiastic about (it),” said Rosburg, who also spoke to every coach she knows that experienced camp in West Virginia. “Especially the ones that know us. Like, ‘Oh you guys are gonna love it. Coach Harbaugh is gonna love it.’ Because they just know we’re gonna take advantage of every opportunity that this place has to offer.”
During training camp, the Giants will stay at The Greenbrier Hotel. But the main benefit isn’t the luxury lodging; it’s what’s down the road from the historic hotel.
Not only do the Giants have access to two grass fields and a FieldTurf field, but also fully equipped meeting rooms, offices, a training room and an on-site weight room, which is a big change from the Giants’ Albany days, when team meetings were held in college classrooms. They also don’t have to bring lockers or weights to set up a weight room.
“What’s nice about this is there’s a lot in place,” said Jim Phelan, a longtime Giants administrator who is now the vice president of team operations. “So, what we have to bring there is less. We don’t have to move our entire weight room. … It’s set up for an NFL team.”
One item that did make the trek from New Jersey was the Giants’ scoreboard, which is vital for practicing situational football and used at every practice. While the equipment staff looked into renting one, they ended up bringing theirs and the Bobcat vehicle used to move it around the field.
Next stop: Training Camp! 🚛 pic.twitter.com/bS8gjyXEIl
— New York Giants (@Giants) July 27, 2026
The movers were able to forklift it onto the truck and off to West Virginia; it went along with other field equipment, including sleds, tackling dummies and everything else the Giants need, and it is now sitting at The Greenbrier’s pristine fields, primed and ready for practice. Even though The Greenbrier is farther away from East Rutherford than Albany, the more complete setup meant a smaller fleet of moving trucks that started the trek south a week before the first practice.
Once there, it was up to several departments to get ready for a travel party of 230-250 people. From remembering whistles and stopwatches to having spare helmets, blank jerseys with numbers, letters and a heat press as well as a seamstress lined up in case the Giants sign a player mid-camp, team staffers tried to prepare for every possible scenario.
Director of performance nutrition Matt Frakes, who joined the Giants in 2025, is already adept at adjusting to changing circumstances, as the Giants’ cafeteria underwent a complete renovation this spring, forcing the team to use a meal tent. So, Frakes’ staff is well-prepared to use The Greenbrier meal tent, which is where the team will eat most meals and start their days.
Making sure his staff can offer everything that’s on the menu in New Jersey at The Greenbrier has been in the works since early this year.
Beyond plenty of conversations between chefs and hospitality staff, a chef from The Greenbrier visited New Jersey during OTAs to observe how much players and staff ate at certain times. The Giants’ executive chef will also be at the resort to ensure players can get familiar favorites.
One way to ensure they can get all the comforts of home was to pass along to The Greenbrier all the purveyors the Giants use, so that the specific types of food, from steaks to produce, will be ordered to West Virginia. Then there are specialty products like beef jerky, protein shake ingredients, electrolytes, hydration items and more, which Frakes has been tracking on an Excel spreadsheet to ensure the team has shipped enough pallets to cover two weeks of practice. While there might be a full team at the resort, individual meal plans and preferences are personalized for every player to account for allergies, injury and other specifics.
“There’s a lot to it aside from just the food service operations part of it,” Frakes said. “You also have the nutrition assessment piece of it. Then you have the strength, conditioning, performance piece of it. So, it’s in buckets, if you will, of how you address it.”

full_text:
How much time does Aaron Glenn have to turn things around? Seth Wenig / AP
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. — Thunder struck and heavy rain pattered as Breece Hall spoke with a smile, a fitting metaphor for these New York Jets. For those on the outside looking in, the Jets — and most iterations of them over the last 15 years, to be fair — have looked like a mess. Aaron Glenn, expected to shepherd in what’s supposed to be a new era, is the face of it. There’s a reason he tops many oddsmakers’ lists of coaches most likely to be fired in 2026.
Glenn’s Jets went 3-14 in his first season as head coach, and at times he looked out of his depth. Press conferences were contentious. Decisions, both in-game and in the offseason , were often questionable. He’s a defensive coach, but his Jets set records for defensive futility. He fired half his coaching staff. He took over defensive play-calling; he called it his “superpower.” He declared Geno Smith would bring the Jets to the “promised land.”
He was mocked and ridiculed. That’s all the rain falling outside.
“Honestly, I think everyone that comes to New York, even though he’s played here before, it’s like: You bite off a little more than you can chew,” Hall said. “You don’t realize it. His first year, he dealt with the high highs and the low of lows.”
Glenn’s messaging to the world isn’t the same as it is inside the locker room. A coach standing at a podium saying he has a plan is hard for a fan or anyone following this team to believe in, especially as Glenn has sometimes been less-than-forthcoming with details about that plan.
What he gives his players is different. Maybe they don’t believe what they’re saying — but Glenn is staking his job on them speaking truth to power.
“You have 90 men in that locker room who would run through a wall for him,” said linebacker Demario Davis.
Said Smith: “AG has done a great job of laying out the blueprint for this team and where he wants to take us. It’s our job to bring that into manifestation. I think he’s an outstanding coach and it’s our job to go prove him right.”
The only person who knows if Glenn is actually on the hot seat is his boss, Jets owner Woody Johnson. This is not the same situation as the one Glenn came from in Detroit, where Lions fans called for Dan Campbell to be fired after a 3-13-1 first season and a 1-6 start in year two. That’s when Lions owner Sheila Ford Hamp held an impromptu news conference to say that Campbell wasn’t going anywhere. Privately, that meant everything to Campbell, and to Glenn. The Lions turned it around, finished 9-8 that season, and are on a four-year run of winning records — something the Jets haven’t done in 10 years, when Smith was still in his first go-round with the team.
Maybe Johnson will show him a similar level of patience. We won’t know that for a while.
For now, training camp kicks off Wednesday with a roster and coaching staff full of new faces, free agents such as Davis who chose the Jets and holdovers such as Hall who signed long-term extensions. By all accounts, they are buying what Glenn is selling.
“He knows what he wants out of the organization, out of the coaches, out of the players,” Hall said. “I just think he’s very to the point and direct. It’s very good for us to see that this is the standard, this is what we have to do, this is how we want to police the locker room, the weight room, practices, everything like that.”
Davis, who played with the New Orleans Saints when Glenn was an assistant coach from 2016 to 2020, said he would follow his head coach “into battle anytime.”
“Just because of the character that he has and the type of person that he is,” Davis said. “I believe leadership isn’t based on title, it’s based on relationships. And he’s a phenomenal leader. I’m not shocked he’s doing a tremendous job being a head coach, setting the culture and direction for this team. … He has a keen vision on what’s expected and what the standard is, and he’s laid that out.”
Davis later emphasized that Glenn “has a phenomenal vision of where this team has to go and what it has to do to get there.”
Only Glenn knows that vision, the plan that everyone talks about. Presumably, it starts Wednesday in training camp. He has this stretch before the season opener on Sept. 13 to finish installing his defense; for offensive coordinator Frank Reich to finish installing his offense; for the new players, rookies and vets to ingratiate themselves with the returning members of the team. Last year’s Jets lacked an identity. They can’t again.
That’s all part of Glenn’s plan. And the path to figuring out whether it’s the right plan starts now.

full_text:
Daronte Jones’ 14th move took him from Minneapolis to suburban Washington, where he is now the defensive coordinator of the Commanders. Nick Wass / Associated Press
LOTHIAN, Md. — Ben Jones Lane is private and dirt, and as it tumbles further into rural Anne Arundel County, Md., it leaves the strip malls of neighboring Prince George’s County — home to the Washington Commanders — behind. Washington, D.C., just more than a half an hour by car, falls further back still.
One stifling afternoon earlier this month, Daronte Jones pulled his 2020 Porsche 911 onto the bumps and the gravel. He has been making this drive his whole life. He slowed down to look at the street sign.
“Ben Jones was my grandfather’s uncle,” Daronte Jones said, fully at a stop. “Or … great uncle? No, uncle. His uncle.”
The Jones clan is both unwieldy and tight. Daronte Jones lived with his mother Darlene — the second-oldest of Calvert and Inez Jones’s seven children — on the Jones’ tobacco farm until he was in third grade. Aunts, uncles and cousins lived in houses strewn across 100 acres.
“I hated farm life,” he said. Still, he knows it shaped him.
Jones is a football coach. The life of a football coach is, by nature, itinerant. He is 47. He has slept under his desk and in his car. He has coached in Maryland (Bowie State) and Montreal (Alouettes). He has coached in the Pac-12 (UCLA), the Big Ten (Wisconsin) and the Mountain West (Hawaii). He has coached at four stops in Louisiana alone (Nicholls State, a pair of high schools and LSU with the big boys). He has coached NFL teams by sea (Dolphins) and by land (Bengals, Vikings).
In a career that spans 26 years, he has moved 14 times. His permanent mailing address through it all: the little house of Calvert and Inez Jones on Ben Jones Lane, tucked away in rural Maryland.
“For the longest time, I would move, and I would never unpack because I was always planning for the next job,” Jones said, standing in the yard in front of his grandparents’ house. “You never really felt like you were settled. You got boxes everywhere, and then when you do unpack, now you’re packing up again.
“It just never felt like you’re home anywhere.”
Jones took a few strides. Some of Calvert Jones’ ducks wandered through the yard, past the pigeon cages, not far from where the basketball court once sat, a few waddles from where Calvert used to keep his pigs, around the corner from Inez’s manicured walkway to the front steps, lined with flowers.
Daronte Jones’ 14th move took him from Minneapolis, where he was the defensive backs coach of the Minnesota Vikings, to suburban Washington, where he is now the defensive coordinator of the Commanders. His new home field, Northwest Stadium, is around the corner from the elementary and middle schools where he first played football. He and his wife moved to McLean, Va., a short drive to the Commanders’ training facility in Ashburn.
It took more than a quarter of a century. But now, when Calvert Jones cooks for the extended family and Inez welcomes them on Sunday afternoons — when the cars are lined up and down Ben Jones Lane — Daronte Jones can join his cousins and aunts and uncles and his mom. After all the time away, he’s back home.
“Here,” he said, “we unpacked.”
As the Commanders prepare for a training camp that opens Wednesday with first-time coordinators on both sides of the ball — David Blough takes over for Kliff Kingsbury on offense, Jones for the fired Joe Whitt Jr. on defense — head coach Dan Quinn was asked what jumped out about Jones in his first few months on the job.
“Just the attention to detail,” Quinn said.
“Details kind of separate you from being average and being really good,” said Ken Norton Jr., the Commanders’ veteran linebackers coach who is working with Jones for the first time. “And he knows his details. He understands that we need to understand what the details are of each and every position and each and every coverage.”
For Jones, that comes from a lifetime in coaching, from the countless mentors and peers who have provided lessons along the way. But it also comes from all that time spent on Ben Jones Lane, where Calvert Jones put young Daronte to work. Calvert is now 86, a carpenter by trade. That deck off his house? Daronte has sweat equity in it, working by Calvert’s side.
The list of chores was endless and all over the map. Daronte toiled in the tobacco fields, since plowed under. Calvert raised beagles — maybe 40 at a time — to help him hunt rabbits. Daronte not only had to help build the dog houses, but was tasked with dragging a pet rabbit through the woods, lacing the trail with its scent, so the beagle puppies could learn to track it down and flush it out.
All those dogs, they had metal dishes in front of their kennels. Daronte’s task: Fill them with water. Simple enough.
“I didn’t clean out the water pan,” Daronte said.
Calvert Jones had standards.
“He’s like, ‘You see this green stuff from the trees? You gotta get that out of there. They can’t drink that,’” Daronte said. “I’m like, ‘Yeah they can. They’re dogs.’”
Calvert dumped the water out of a bowl. He reached up to an overhanging tree branch, ripped off some leaves and used them as a rag to clean out the bowl. He then filled it with water, proper for his beloved beagles.
“For me, when I was young, it was like, it doesn’t really matter — you know what I mean?” Jones said. “But what he really taught me then: Everything matters.”
Over the phone, Brian Flores, the well-respected defensive coordinator of the Vikings, ticked off the virtues and talents of Daronte Jones, his former defensive backs coach. He’s creative, not afraid to test the limits, has a great way of relating to players — all the stuff you’d expect a boss to say when extolling the virtues of an understudy who advanced.
Then he landed on a greater truth.
“We call him the Renaissance Man,” Flores said.
“I mean, he’s the best-dressed guy in the building,” Flores said. “He’s got the best bags and luggage. He’s the most traveled. He has been all over the world.”
As Jones drove that Porsche 911 through the back roads of Maryland, wearing a white linen shirt and black shorts, he was freshly back from his first real visit to Japan. He took in the crowds at Shibuya Crossing in the heart of Tokyo. He carefully selected his seat on the bullet train to Osaka so he’d be positioned for the best view of Mount Fuji. Alas, it was clouded over.
Another time. Because there’s always another trip. Jones tries to leave the country twice a year.
“I love seeing people at their best, in their own surroundings,” he said. “It just opens up so many different experiences. You know, sometimes when we’re here, we can be absorbed by — you can call it the rat race.”
Some football coaches almost pride themselves on having little life beyond the game. Jones revels in exploring outside of football. When he spent three years on the staff at Hawaii, Norm Chow, the well-traveled head coach of the Rainbow Warriors, encouraged him to see the world, telling him, “You want to spend money on experiences and memories.”
“I think it’s a big, big world we’re living in out there, right?” Chow said by phone this month. “And the fact that he was already halfway to Asia, and that part of the world is a little easier to get to, made sense. To his credit, he took advantage of that.”
Jones’ first international trip was to Zurich. He was so ill-prepared for the experience that he was taken aback by signs that weren’t in English.
“The survival skills kicked in,” Jones said. “And I have not stopped since.”
Geneva, Milan and Venice followed on that trip. South Africa, Australia, an emotional trip to Israel and Jordan with his mother, aunt and grandmother — on which he was re-baptized — came later. He even won over his now-wife by revealing he had been to the country of her roots, Taiwan.
“She’s like, ‘No, Taiwan , not Thailand,’” Jones said. “I was like, ‘Right. I’ve been to Taipei. I went there by myself on vacation.’ I think that…

title: Cardinals Camp Notebook, Day 5: Pads On, Physicality Up
full_text:
GLENDALE — Lights. Camera. Action.
The pads came on for the first time today at State Farm Stadium as the Cardinals now progress into the second phase of training camp.
There's a different sense of physicality when the pads come on as the rushing attack is able to gain a better and more realistic feel as opposed to the initial days of camp - where Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur dubbed it a "passing camp" to begin festivities.
A recap from a busy (and brusing) day in the desert:
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur on ramping up the physicality up with pads:
"There's going to be collisions out there, obviously, and when the ball carrier is going, particularly between the tackles, and there's opportunities to thud up frontal, they'll do that. And then they'll let them go, and then the shots will come.
"I told the guys if anyone in the hole has a shot to thud them up, thud them up. I don't want to see 11 guys thudding up. That's not realistic. So let them go, and then go get your shot on the ball so that you're 1: you're training yourself and 2: you're training the [running] backs. If it's out in open space or a ball's thrown over the middle, those guys got to be pros. I mean, they're the elite of the elite out there, and guys got to know how to practice.
"Typically the guys that don't know how to practice are the guys that just can't stick around because they're not capable of it. I look forward to seeing them be physical but being smart at the same time."
The Cardinals are back in action tomorrow on Wednesday, July 29, with practice beginning at 4:00 PM.

title: Marvin Harrison Jr. Injury Update Gives Cardinals Fans Sigh of Relief
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals saw star receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. deal with multiple injuries during their last training camp practice, which raised some concerns over his health.
After the team had a scheduled day off on Monday, the Cardinals are back to work, and it appears Harrison should be just fine.
"Cramping. Yep. He's totally good. He was cramping," Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur said of Harrison ahead of Tuesday's practice, where pads are set to come on for the first time.
Harrison initially was spotted hobbling early in Sunday's practice before later landing awkwardly on his side.
Marvin Harrison Jr. has been in some obvious discomfort since coming down with a sideline catch during team drills. Cards have tomorrow off before returning to action on Tuesday. pic.twitter.com/mXbDseFWGc
Harrison's entering a critical third season in the league after his initial stint in Arizona has seen highs and lows. The No. 4 overall pick, once labeled generational, now faces a massive season where there's hope LaFleur can maximize his talents.
In a crowded Cardinals pass-catchers room that also features Trey McBride and Michael Wilson, Harrison will have ample opportunity to establish himself – though there won't be a defined WR1 in Arizona.
"You just try to put them in those positions. Who [receiver] one is number one on the progression for that play. And you're trying to do that balancing act of like, hey, we got talent. Don't overthink this thing. Don't try to get too schemy. Let these guys go out and play fast [and] do what they do well," LaFleur said.
"But at the same time, [we need to] put them in positions where you know it's not a dead play, if you will. So there's a lot of lot of elements to it.
"There's so much to it in terms of putting these guys in positions that we think they're going to be successful within the scheme that we're trying to get done and the defense that we're going against."
Harrison is coming off a season where he suffered from appendicitis, two heel injuries and a concussion — causing him to miss five games. He told reporters he still wasn't 100% healthy back in June when mandatory minicamp was rolling.
"I go 100% [during practice]. I'm still out there doing everything I normally would do, but yeah, it's just like an ongoing process for sure," Harrison said.
The Cardinals are entering their fifth practice of 2026's training camp period. Their first preseason action will come on Thursday, Aug. 6 in the NFL's Hall of Fame Game against the Carolina Panthers.

title: Jeremiyah Love Is Already Turning Heads at Arizona Cardinals Camp
full_text:
ARIZONA — $50 million can get you far in life. Oftentimes, no amount of money can buy love, but for the Arizona Cardinals, they've been nothing short of heart eyes over their star rookie.
Rookie running back Jeremiyah Love has very much looked the part of a playmaker through the early stages of his Cardinals tenure. It's tough for running backs to really establish themselves in training camp — without pads — but Love's been able to do just that.
“Obviously, I haven’t met with Jeremiyah yet,” Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett said. “But being able to be here and watch him practice and do his thing — I see why we paid him $50 million."
I would not have a linebacker in coverage on Jeremiyah Love pic.twitter.com/h33HLQTqkF
Love, the third overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, has earned every bit of praise since first stepping foot in the team's facility. The way he carries himself off the field in terms of maturity and leadership has only been countered by the lighting-quick agility and vision he's displayed early on at State Farm Stadium.
A three-win team drafting a running back that high typically is laughed at — and the Cardinals surely were on the end of online backlash from media and fans alike following the pick. Rarely does a player at a devalued position truly make a difference, though Arizona believes Love is a rare weapon capable of doing damage as both a runner and pass-catcher.
Jeremiyah Love’s initial burst is just different man. pic.twitter.com/VCk5D51Qtf
ESPN's Matt Bowen ranked Love's pick 12th out of the most impactful moves made this offseason across the entire league:
"Love should be viewed as a three-down playmaker, similar to how Jahmyr Gibbs was seen as a rookie with the Lions. Love scored 21 total touchdowns for Notre Dame in 2025, and he was a home run hitter with 39 rushes of 10 or more yards. Plus, Love had 63 receptions during his college career, and his route tree should expand in the Cardinals' offense."
Love doesn't project as a bellcow back. That's not what head coach Mike LaFleur has deployed previously at other stops and that's not likely to change with Tyler Allgeier and James Conner firmly in the mix.
He also won't be a savior of the franchise. That's far too heavy of a weight for any rookie to carry, let alone a running back.
However, he's been everything as advertised through the early stages of camp, and that should continue as the pads come on today.

title: 5 Brutally Honest Thoughts on Jacoby Brissett's New Cardinals Contract
full_text:
ARIZONA — The deed is done.
The Arizona Cardinals handed Jacoby Brissett a significant pay raise ahead of the 2026 season, satisfying the veteran ahead of his final year in the desert while ending his hold-in and gaining the presumed starter back in the mix.
Five brutally honest thoughts on Brissett's contract, and where we go from here:
We previously touched on this , but if we're going to anoint a clear winner from this process, it's Brissett.
He might have been the first quarterback in league history to have started 12 games on a three-win team and successfully held out for a more lucrative extension that is now paying him nearly three times as much — without incentives.
At 33 years old, this was likely Brissett's final opportunity at a lucrative contract with starting duties in mind, and he made the most of it even without an agent to represent him during talks.
Brissett went toe-to-toe with the Cardinals and ultimately walked away with $15.5 million guaranteed and opportunity to earn up to $21 million.
Arizona hasn't played a game yet, though Brissett's 1-0 already in 2026.
Shifting into a front office perspective, it's not as if the Cardinals were taken to the woodshed.
Are the optics of paying Brissett bad from the outside? Surely, and they'll continue to face heat for it well into the regular season. That being said, the Cardinals are confident in Brissett's ability to manage Mike LaFleur's new offense.
$15.5 million is nothing for a starting quarterback, which is what Arizona believes they have. He did go 1-11 as the Cardinals' starter last year, though beyond box score scouting it's clear Brissett isn't a bad quarterback. He kept the offense going on time, spread the ball out and didn't turn the ball over at a high rate.
If all cylinders are firing in LaFleur's offense, that's all you can really ask for out of a quarterback at this point in time.
No new years were added to Brissett's deal, either. Arizona can rinse their hands from the veteran after this year and march forward into the future, which could involve their third-round pick.
Yes, the Cardinals paid Brissett. Much more money. And yes, Arizona undoubtedly will start him to begin the season.
However, Brissett's reworked deal won't preclude the Cardinals from pulling him out of the starting lineup if Arizona's again in the basement of NFL standings, especially with massive questions needing to be answered on Beck ahead of a potentially bountiful 2027 quarterback class.
Brissett's $15 million figure isn't quite the mammoth figure fans make it out to be in the grand scheme of Arizona's salary cap picture. The Cardinals, if bad enough, will make a change at quarterback.
As for Beck, he's struggled a bit early in camp but will need live reps during the regular season, as many as possible, before the Cardinals can feel confident in making an assessment on their rookie quarterback.
That's a decision that could change the franchise's trajectory. The Cardinals know that, and if they enter the 2027 offseason without having seen Beck play, either Arizona shocked the world with how competitive they were or the Cardinals have to essentially guess on their future of football's most important position.
Where does all of this leave veteran free agent signing Gardner Minshew?
Available for trade, that's where. That's not to say the Cardinals will be itching to offload Minshew at the first opportunity, though Arizona will surely find themselves in a position where a team who, perhaps suffered an injury at quarterback, wants to get a cheap but experienced stopgap.
With Brissett now firmly in the driver's seat and the aforementioned Beck situation needing attention, Minshew finds himself in the middle of a quarterback sandwich where he's not going to be a key ingredient.
If the price is right, perhaps a contending team will lose their star and want to pay up for Brissett. However, Minshew is by far the most likely candidate to go around the trade deadline — which is odd considering he's looked the best of any quarterback during camp.
I've been fairly critical of Brissett through this process, calling the contract standoff laughable earlier in the offseason. His words after inking the deal — where he told reporters he couldn't care less about people who questioned him and his decision to ask for a raise — also ruffled some feathers .
Brissett is somebody who is very much, and unapologetically, himself. He's not quite a PR nightmare and he doesn't actually say or do anything questionable, but he's always been blunt in terms of his words and opinions.
It's so easy to repeat a media-trained answer while taking the high road, so we appreciate athletes who are actually open and honest in front of a microphone instead of regurgitating the same answer time and time again.
Even if Brissett isn't a fan-favorite, his boldness and honesty is respectable in world that doesn't see much of that anymore.

title: Who's Next? Cardinals Extension Candidates After Jacoby Brissett's New Contract
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals finally have Jacoby Brissett under contract after a long offseason of negotiations.
Brissett inked a nice $15.5 million in guarantees as Cardinals training camp marches forward into the future, finally putting to rest Arizona's most prominent contract standoff.
However, the Cardinals are far from done with players who need new deals.
Ranking, in no order, the top Cardinals next in line for a payday after Brissett:
Some fans speculated Johnson was nearing a deal after he began training camp on the PUP list, though he's now healthy with no extension in sight.
There's not a rush to get a deal done with the former No. 6 overall pick, as Johnson had his fifth-year option picked up on his rookie deal, ensuring he stays with the Cardinals through 2027.
However, Arizona would be wise to strike a deal with Johnson before the market continues to rise for players at left tackle — one of the league's more premium positions. Johnson is worthy of a contract extension and should be an achor for Arizona's line for years to come.
He made some comments about wanting $40 million per season, though that would be $10 million more than the highest at his position in Leramy Tunsil.
Wilson is entering the final year of his rookie contract fresh off his most productive season, though there's some hesitation with paying the Stanford product.
Wilson's career production has essentially all came within the last ten or so games of 2025. While he burst on the scene after a slow start to have 1,000 yards receiving, some are hesitant to pay him off a small window of production.
To that, we say Wilson has always produced when the ball was thrown his way — he simply didn't have the ample opportunity he did last season. Now, with new head coach Mike LaFleur installing a new offense, there's hope Wilson is able to take a massive step in 2026.
Are the Cardinals wanting to wait to strike a deal with Wilson? Is that bet only going to grow more expensive if Wilson again shows out and produces? These are questions general manager Monti Ossenfort has to wrestle with.
Don't let recent injuries fool you, Williams is one of the NFL's best slot cornerbacks and is a valuable piece to this Cardinals defense. Defensive coordinator Nick Rallis uses Williams in a plethora of roles thanks to his football IQ, athleticism and positional versatility.
However, injuries do unfortunately play a part in contract talks with the Cardinals. Had Williams stayed healthy entering the offseason, an extension felt like a no-brainer. That might still be the case, though Williams' arrival to the PUP list at the start of camp from his season-ending Achilles injury last year might give Arizona some hesitation.
The Cardinals may be willing to offer a lower number for Williams to sign now, or they may be wanting to revisit negotations at the end of the regular season.
If Williams returns to previous form, this feels like an obvious choice for a Cardinals cornerback room that has exciting but unproven talent.

title: Biggest Winner of Jacoby Brissett, Cardinals Contract Saga Was Obvious
full_text:
ARIZONA — The dust is beginning to settle on Jacoby Brissett's restructured contract with the Arizona Cardinals.
Brissett and the Cardinals had been engaged since the early stages of the offseason, where Arizona parted from Kyler Murray and wiped the quarterback slate clean. It's obvious the 33-year-old isn't in the franchise's future plans, though an upgrade to the contract was still needed if he was still going to be the team's starter.
That got done, four days after the Cardinals initially reported to training camp last week.
"Happy for him. Happy for our team. It was productive, you know, and for it to get done now, sooner rather than later, is good," Cardinals coach Mike LaFleur said .
Like anywhere else in life, there's winners and losers. The Cardinals aren't quite losers walking away from the negotiation table, but it's hard not to see Brissett as the massive winner here.
Brissett's re-worked deal added no years to his contract (where he'll be a free agent in 2027) with a now $15.5 million fully guaranteed contract with incentives that could lead to $21 million, per reports.
To be clear, it's not as if the Cardinals got taken to the cleaners here. $15.5 million is very cheap in the big picture of starting quarterback money, and in their eyes, Brissett is capable of steadying the ship.
"I think he has the ability to throw it at all three levels," LaFleur said of Brissett.
Arizona's not on the hook for Brissett past this season, and quite honestly if Brissett still can't get the Cardinals back into the win column, that figure isn't enough to make Arizona hesitate on throwing somebody like Carson Beck in the lineup.
This isn't a massive deal for Arizona. They had plenty of cap space to facilitate a new and more lucrative deal for Brissett.
However, this was a massive win for Brissett based off circumstances alone.
Brissett almost triples the amount of cash he's due in 2026, jumping from $5.4 million to $15.5 million with potential to earn more. His incentives are not known at this time, though he now has the ninth-most guaranteed money for a starting quarterback ( h/t ESPN ).
He also negotiated the deal without an agent, though he told reporters on Sunday he had a team of people to reference throughout negotiations.
"I think that's the business of this league," Brissett said when asked what led to the eventual hold-in for a new contract during camp. He was not present during offseason team activities and was off to the side during mandatory minicamp.
"I think it kind of just unfolds as the business side goes."
Brissett won't be here in 2027. The Cardinals very much have their eyes set to the future of the position, and both parties have an understanding of what Brissett is: A bridge. A placeholder. A temporary fill-in that can function at a high enough level to give your offense a chance.
Yet there's just something about a contract standoff between a quarterback who won just one of twelve starts last season and a team who finished 3-14 that made so much of the public scratch their heads when news of Brissett's demands first came to light.
As for the starting record, Brissett said he, "couldn't care less" about those who didn't think he deserved the money.
He's got 15 million reasons not to care, and at the end of the day, Brissett ultimately got what he wanted from a team that was clearly desperate to have him in the mix.

title: Jacoby Brissett 'Couldn't Care Less' About Cardinals Holdout Critics
full_text:
GLENDALE — Jacoby Brissett wanted to have his cake and eat it, too.
Brissett landed a lucrative (and reworked) contract for the 2026 season that sees his guaranteed total rise to $15 million, far from the $1.5 million he initially entered the offseason with. After months of negotiations, Brissett emerges as a major winner.
He joked with reporters about having cake in the locker room to celebrate before revealing the reaction from his teammates meant more to him than the actual contract getting done.
Brissett's been at the end of plenty of online jokes since rumors first surfaced early in the offseason of his desire for a new deal. In spite of throwing for a career-best in categories such as yards/touchdowns, Brissett led the Cardinals to just one win in 12 outings in 2025.
That, combined with Arizona's 3-14 record, placed a unique set of circumstances around the holdout. On paper, you don't see that scenario play out very often — if at all.
After Brissett got his paper, he wasn't shy when asked about the people who were skeptical of his holdout.
"I couldn't care less. Deal got done."
Later at practice, Brissett took team snaps for the first time all training camp after being a bystander at offseason team activities and mandatory minicamp.
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur confirmed to reporters that Brissett is in the plans to be the team's starter to begin the season, and will take over said duties as soon as Tuesday. Arizona has a scheduled off day on Monday.
"We want to still get him up to speed in terms of not just schematically — I'm really not even worried about that with him because of what I've always told you guys. He doesn't need to learn defense. Doesn't need to learn the speed of the game. Doesn't even really need to learn our players per se," LaFleur said this morning.
Brissett is still set to be a scheduled free agent after this season, though now all eyes are fixated on getting back on track with the Cardinals' offense.
Which first requires a good night's rest.
"I'm pretty sure I'll probably sleep more than three hours tonight, and we got an off day tomorrow, so I'll sleep in a little bit," Brissett told reporters after practice.
No matter how you slice the cake, Brissett's officially back in the saddle as Arizona's starting quarterback. Now, it's up to him to prove how sweet things can be.
